identification.summary: UNC2814 is a suspected PRC-nexus cyber espionage group that Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant have tracked since 2017, primarily targeting telecommunications providers and also government organizations [S1]. As of 18 February 2026 GTIG confirmed 53 victims in 42 countries across four continents, with suspected infections in at least 20 more countries [S1]. The group uses the GRIDTIDE backdoor, which abuses the Google Sheets API as a command-and-control channel [S1].
identification.firstObserved: GTIG has tracked UNC2814 since 2017 [S1]. VPN configuration metadata suggests SoftEther infrastructure in use as early as July 2018 [S1].
identification.notes: UNC2814 is a Google/Mandiant uncertain-cluster designation, not a Microsoft or MITRE name; no Microsoft name or MITRE group ID is cited in the sources gathered. GTIG states it observed no overlap with Salt Typhoon, which it describes as having different victims and TTPs, despite the shared telecom focus [S1][S2]. Google's blog conclusion cites 'over 70 countries' for confirmed or suspected operations, which does not match its body text (42 confirmed plus at least 20 suspected, about 62) [S1].

attribution.confidence: GTIG describes the group as 'suspected' PRC-nexus; the sources gathered state no specific PRC agency, contractor or government attribution [S1].
attribution.basis: Google's characterization rests on its own long-term tracking and telemetry; the sources gathered do not publish the underlying evidence for the PRC-nexus assessment [S1].

objectives: GTIG assesses the access would enable call data record theft, SMS monitoring and abuse of lawful intercept capabilities, potentially to surveil dissidents, activists and traditional espionage targets; GTIG did not directly observe data exfiltration in this campaign [S1][S2].

regions: 53 confirmed victims in 42 countries across four continents, including Africa, Asia and the Americas [S1][S3]
Suspected infections in at least 20 additional countries [S1]
targeting.notes: One compromised endpoint held PII including full name, phone number, date and place of birth, voter ID and national ID numbers [S1]. Many victims were likely compromised for years, and GTIG could not confirm GRIDTIDE was used in every intrusion [S2]. Specific victim countries and organizations are not named in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: GRIDTIDE is a C-based ELF backdoor that executes shell commands and uploads and downloads files, using the Google Sheets API for cell-based C2 (command polling and status in cell A1, data transfer in A2:An, host metadata in V1), with data encoded in URL-safe Base64 and configuration decrypted with AES-128-CBC [S1]. Intrusions showed SSH lateral movement with a service account, living-off-the-land reconnaissance and privilege escalation, persistence via a systemd unit (xapt.service launching /usr/sbin/xapt), and SoftEther VPN Bridge for encrypted outbound connections [S1]. Payload archives were hosted on 130.94.6[.]228 [S1]. Initial access was not determined, though the group has a history of exploiting web servers and edge systems [S1]. Google states GRIDTIDE abuses documented Sheets API behavior rather than a product vulnerability [S2].

campaigns.name: GRIDTIDE disruption
campaigns.summary: GTIG and partners terminated attacker-controlled Google Cloud projects, disabled accounts and Sheets API access, sinkholed current and historical domains, notified victims and deployed detections; blog published 25 February 2026 reporting 53 confirmed victims in 42 countries. GTIG expects UNC2814 to try to rebuild its footprint.

diamond.adversary: Suspected PRC-nexus cluster tracked by GTIG since 2017; sponsor not specified [S1].
diamond.capability: GRIDTIDE backdoor, SoftEther VPN Bridge, SSH lateral movement, systemd persistence, living-off-the-land tools [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Google Sheets API C2 using attacker-controlled Google service accounts and cloud projects (since disabled); SoftEther VPN servers; dynamic-DNS-style C2 domains; payload host 130.94.6[.]228 [S1].
diamond.victim: Telecommunications providers and government organizations in 42 confirmed countries [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Access consistent with signals-intelligence style collection on communications and surveillance of dissidents and activists, per GTIG's assessment [S1].
diamond.technology: Linux servers (a CentOS host was observed) in telecom environments, internet-facing web and edge systems, and trusted cloud API traffic that blends with legitimate use [S1].

gaps: No sponsor, agency or contractor attribution is published in the sources gathered; 'suspected PRC-nexus' is Google's assessment only [S1].
No direct exfiltration observed; actual data loss is unknown [S1].
Victim names and countries were not published in the sources gathered.
Whether GRIDTIDE was used in every intrusion is unconfirmed [S2].
Discrepancy between 'over 70 countries' in Google's conclusion and about 62 in its body [S1].
Relationship to other PRC telecom-targeting clusters (Salt Typhoon, others) is stated by Google as no observed overlap; not independently verified [S1][S2].
Post-disruption activity or rebuilding by UNC2814 not found in searches run.
Full IOC table is in Google's GTI collection, which was not opened; WebFetch of The Hacker News and SecurityWeek failed (host unreachable).

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Telecom core and management Linux servers, and the SSH service accounts that reach them, are key cyber terrain because access enables call-record and SMS collection and lawful-intercept abuse [S1]. STEP 2: The actor blends C2 into legitimate Google Sheets API traffic and uses SoftEther VPN, so network allow-listing of major cloud APIs offers little protection [S1]. STEP 3: The sourced pattern is edge or web-server access (suspected, not confirmed), then SSH lateral movement with a service account, systemd persistence, SoftEther tunnel and GRIDTIDE [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is quiet persistence in telecom and government networks in many countries for collection on communications data; MDCOA is rebuilding on new cloud services after the February 2026 disruption and using telecom access against coalition partner or host-nation networks [S1]. Candidate indicators: shell processes spawned from /var/tmp, unexpected xapt.service systemd units, non-browser processes calling sheets.googleapis.com (batchClear, batchUpdate), and SoftEther VPN Bridge traffic from Linux servers [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track host-nation and partner telecom exposure, since victims span at least 42 countries and many were likely compromised for years [S1][S2]. (2) Authorities: coordination with commercial providers (Google disrupted infrastructure and notified victims) runs through provider and partner channels rather than DoD authorities; confirm legal basis before any action on partner networks [S1]. (3) Mission assurance: DoD reliance on commercial and host-nation telecom for command and control and communications should be assessed for lawful-intercept abuse risk and for exposure of personnel PII [S1]. (4) Coordination: share the published Google IOCs and detection rules with network defenders and expect rebuilt infrastructure [S1].
